title: japans massive quake kills 25 people 2026 07 30
text:
Hello,
Tragedy struck southern Japan this week as a 7.1-magnitude earthquake toppled houses and split open streets in the small city of Yatsushiro.
The Kumamoto prefectural government said the death toll from the earthquake was now at 25, with the majority of them at Nippon Paper Industries' paper mill, which suffered major structural damage, and at Aeon's shopping mall, where a possible gas explosion occurred.
Nine other deaths in the prefecture were being investigated to ascertain if they were linked to the quake, it said.
The quake’s ​epicenter was about 20 km (12 miles) south of Kumamoto City, central Kyushu's largest city with a population of around 700,000. The quake has been followed by more than 100 small aftershocks that continued through Wednesday.
Lack of ‌water and power
There was mounting concern about invisible threats from the lack of water and power amid the punishing summer heat.
Many of the port city's roughly 58,000 households were still without running water or power on Thursday.
A Kumamoto official warned of the risk of heat stroke with temperatures that were forecast to reach close to 40 C at the weekend. The Reuters Climate Monitor shows that Kumamoto is currently 34 degrees Celsius (94 degrees Fahrenheit) which is 4.1 C above its historical average.
Japan's military, the Self-Defense Forces (SDF), is installing about 300 air-conditioning units in evacuation centers and other key sites around Kumamoto.
With the city hall's ​toilets out of order, officials erected emergency toilets over sewer manholes outside the building, in temperatures of around 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit) and stifling humidity.
A Kyushu Electric Power representative said the utility was aiming to restore power by ​Friday evening.
Tragedy at the mall
One of the hardest hit areas was the Aeon shopping mall.
Hundreds of shoppers and store employees, quickly ushered by staff to evacuate, watched on in horror as an explosion ripped ⁠through the building, exposing the structure's steel beams and catapulting debris across the parking lot.
The mall, the biggest in the prefecture, had just reopened last month as a new and improved shopping and entertainment complex to commemorate its recovery from another deadly tremor ​a decade ago.
After being badly damaged in the magnitude 7.3 Kumamoto earthquake in April 2016, the operator highlighted its seismically reinforced ceilings and overall improvements to safety and resilience as part of its redevelopment.
Aeon President Akio Yoshida told a press conference on Wednesday that ​staff evacuated 3,000 shoppers within half an hour after the quake hit. But an unlucky few were inside when, 50 minutes later, the explosion occurred.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said it was a "race against time" to rescue those still trapped in the mall and others affected by the quake. Around 170 soldiers have been deployed to help with rescue operations at the site.
Located on the "Ring of Fire" of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling the Pacific Basin, Japan accounts for about 20% of the world's earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or more.
The massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and ​injured a further 2,739, according to an official count, and damaged thousands of buildings including the walls of the city's castle, a top tourist site.
* Talking Points
* In Conversation
In keeping with the ESG Lens focus on boardroom diversity, a report by U.S.-based shareholder representatives As You Sow showed that diverse management is associated with stronger revenue growth, returns, and share prices.
As You Sow ​analyzed over one million EEO-1 data points across 1,482 publicly traded U.S. companies between 2016 and 2024. EEO-1 is a mandatory U.S. government survey requiring certain employers to submit workforce demographic ​data, specifically covering race, ethnicity, and ⁠gender.
The analysis found that greater representation of Black, Indigenous, and people of color in management was significantly and positively associated with income after tax, five- and 10-year revenue growth, return on equity, return on invested capital, free cash flow per share, and five- and 10-year share price appreciation.
The positive link to income after tax and ROIC was seen from 2016 through 2019, four years before the surge in corporate diversity commitments that followed the murder of George Floyd in 2020.
By direct contrast, increases in White male management representation showed the most consistently negative association ⁠with aggregate financial ​performance across broad financial metrics.
"This is not about White men,” said Andrew Behar, CEO of As You Sow, himself a White man. “It's about what happens when ​a management team thinks the same way.
“Homogeneous leadership tends to share the same blind spots, miss the same risks, and reach for the same familiar answers, and over time, that shows up in financial results.
“The data indicates that investors who wanted their portfolios to outperform between 2016-2024 could have bet on diverse management teams.”
